title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
description: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. The remainin
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack.Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they meanThe company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

schema.headline: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack

title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
description: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows. Eight of 26 provinces are
body: More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows. Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak. Testing and treatment are under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added. The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain. DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said. The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate". Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing. Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

schema.headline: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak

title: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
description: Warning: This story contains graphic content.Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few
body: Warning: This story contains graphic content.Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive."We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on buses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday. On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers. For many, there were emotional reunions. Tetiana and Volodymyr, a couple carrying a cat when they arrived in Chernihiv, said their entire home was burned down three years ago, and they had been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour since.For them, leaving as soon as it was safe to do so was an easy decision. "There's nothing for us to regret leaving. We don't have relatives there. Our children are married and don't live with us in the city," said Tetiana.But those who managed to escape also worry about those left behind. "There are still a lot of people left there, living under those conditions," said Olha.Now that the evacuees have left Oleshky, they will also face a new challenge - working out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.Palii said he would look for a job so he can provide for his family: "There's no job I can't handle. Digging, hoeing, planting, building. I can even do demolition work."Olha said she and her family have no relatives elsewhere in Ukraine, and they will stay with some acquaintances for an extended period while they get back on their feet."If we managed to survive in hell, we'll survive here too."

schema.headline: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city

title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
description: In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,00
body: In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night.He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day".The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel. The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east. Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio."Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

schema.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

title: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentRepo
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentReporting fromBangkokEven before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending."To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prisonThe past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions."If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arnon at a protest in 2023From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son."Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom." Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.That changed on 3 August 2020.That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughterOne of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame. She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy."I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve."I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté."It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."Image source, GoodmondayshootImage caption, Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power."We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail. Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves."In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.Image source, Arnon NampaImage caption, Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years agoAs the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs. This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom."Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."

schema.headline: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years

title: Lucy Harrison death: Mum told UK police have 'no authority' in US
description: The grand jury had decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Kris Harrison said the Glock handgun discharged accidentall
body: The grand jury had decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Kris Harrison said the Glock handgun discharged accidentally while he was showing it to his daughter.In February, a coroner in England concluded Lucy had been unlawfully killed, finding that her father's actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter under UK law.Police in Texas have, however, said they would not reopen the investigation.Evans said the force was "ultimately constrained by legal, jurisdictional and practical realities that significantly limit what any police force in England and Wales can do in relation to a death that occurred in the United States," he said.Given the "unusual circumstances reported" of Lucy's death, a Senior Investigating Officer had been tasked with looking into the case. That officer appointed a Family Liaison Officer and sought information from the relevant United States law enforcement agencies.He said that despite the "clear jurisdictional limitations," the force's actions "reflected our recognition of the exceptional circumstances of the case and our commitment to providing whatever support and assistance was realistically available."The family had argued that as Kris Harrison is a British citizen, a mechanism exists under certain circumstances, where those from the United Kingdom who commit murder or manslaughter, can be prosecuted before British courts. In response, Evans said: "Even where jurisdiction may arguably exist in law, the practical ability to investigate and prosecute remains severely constrained when the suspect, witnesses, exhibits and evidential opportunities are all located overseas."No parent should have to endure the loss of a child in such tragic circumstances, and I fully appreciate that the passage of time does not diminish the family's need for answers or their determination to understand exactly what happened to Lucy," Evans added.Coates' lawyer Radd Seiger, has since said the family had "serious concerns" about the investigation and whether all the relevant evidence was properly gathered and considered.He added that further information, including a recent download from Lucy's mobile phone,  contained information which "we believe are relevant to the circumstances leading up to her death".Seiger said: "We are not asking Cheshire Constabulary to take over an American investigation or to determine what happened in Texas."Instead, he said, they were asking the force "to obtain and examine relevant evidence which has not yet been properly investigated"."The family have spent nearly two years trying to get answers about Lucy's death and justice for her. "They are not prepared to accept that the investigation is complete simply because the American authorities have decided not to take the matter further," he added.

schema.headline: Lucy Harrison death: Mum told UK police have 'no authority' in US

title: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
description: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentiall
body: The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise. In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.  Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour. In a BBC interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election. It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers. "There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said. "I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages.""I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."

schema.headline: John Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers

title: Sir Keir Starmer: Europe can't rely on US to 'bankroll' defence, Dublin event told
description: Sir Keir Starmer has said Europe should build a common security framework, warning the change in its defence relationship with the US is permanent rat
body: Sir Keir Starmer has said Europe should build a common security framework, warning the change in its defence relationship with the US is permanent rather than "an aberration of the Trump presidency".The former prime minister was speaking at a British Irish Chamber of Commerce (BICC) dinner in Dublin, external on Friday evening.Sir Keir said a "common security framework" for Europe was needed as much as a common market, with the UK at its centre.He warned that "things will not go back to the way they were," adding that the US had made clear it will no longer "bankroll" its European allies.Press Association reported that he told the crowd in Dublin City Hall his comments did not mean "the US relationship is no longer important".Rather he said the UK-USA military, security and intelligence alliance was "far too strong for that".But he said Europe must be enabled to "take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security".Trump says Nato's new 5% defence spending pledge a 'big win'"Europe has twice been caught asleep – failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events," he said."First when Russia's attack on Ukraine exposed long-standing European weaknesses on defence and security; and second when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up," he added.He added: "I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.Sir Keir was at the dinner to be awarded an honorary life membership from the BICC.

schema.headline: Sir Keir Starmer: Europe can't rely on US to 'bankroll' defence, Dublin event told

title: 'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out
description: Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors finalThe winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no
body: Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors finalThe winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no longer need to keep the biggest secret in British TV, as they reunited to celebrate their victory.Actor Sebastian Croft and comedian Romesh Ranganathan were the last ones standing, with the two faithfuls splitting the £83,000 prize pot between their chosen charities."I am feeling good, it's so nice to finally be able to talk about it properly," Croft, known to pals as Bash, told BBC Newsbeat.The second series of the hit BBC One show finished on Friday, after the original 21 celebs were whittled down to seven finalists.Reuniting with Ranganathan on the comedian's BBC Radio 2 show on Saturday morning, Croft said they had been worried about being seen together in public before the final."We were having dinner and we're not exactly a likely duo and the whole restaurant was like, 'we like you on Traitors and hope you win'," he said.Croft added that he had woken up on Saturday "with a light sense that I don't have to keep the secret anymore. It's been killing me".Ranganathan, 48, started his show by saying: "Last night, I don't know if you're aware, was the finale of The Celebrity Traitors and I won."He said he was "delighted to win" but admitted he probably wouldn't have done so without Croft convincing him to banish the last remaining traitor, King Kenny."It's taken the gloss off it slightly that everybody's saying, 'you better thank [Croft] every day for the rest of your life'," he added, with his typical deadpan-humour.But 24-year-old Croft said he thought Ranganathan had played the game in a "lovely" way."People are seeing how smart you are and how you're actually so on it, and you're such a good judge of character," he praised.Kenny said he "experienced everything possible in the game" after starting out as a faithful, getting a shield to protect him from murder and then being recruited as a traitor.But he said he "should have had a better plan for the final" and wasn't prepared for how hard it would be."There were so many times when I felt bad pinning stuff on people," he said. "It's a very draining thing to do as a traitor. "There's moments when there is fun but lying to people for that long is insane, you build friendships as well and feel bad."On his show, Ranganathan also asked fellow finalist, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock, about taking part in challenges while pregnant. In the final episode, Pinnock was seen hanging off the side of a helicopter and lowering herself to the ground with a rope."I'm just super proud of myself," she said. "It's kind of just shown me that I really can do anything I put my mind to."

schema.headline: 'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out

title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but rules out reparations
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chairwoman Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. As King Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities. On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments. "I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in a piece for the Guardian, external.He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation". He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."Chancellor John Healey told the BBC that Burnham was "open to a discussion" about an apology because it was "the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth heads conference". The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting starts on 1 November in Antigua, and will be opened by the King as part of his tour. Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, Healey said the prime minister does not think reparations are the right approach.He added that a formal apology doesn't mean British people should now "accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago in which they had no role".Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born."In a post on X, Badenoch wrote that Labour was "already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare."Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said: "I do think we have a duty there and saying sorry is always quite a good thing."Bell Ribeiro-Addy said that while her parliamentary group welcomed the government's acceptance of the role it played, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing"."Acknowledgement is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footing… it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."Ribeiro-Addy, who is MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point."My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow. Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough."The British government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now," he said. "This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice." From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.Burnham is not first UK prime minister to address the issue. In 2007, the then PM Tony Blair said the UK's role in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".David Cameron ruled out making reparations for Britain's role in the historic slave trade in 2015, urging Caribbean countries to "move on" during a visit to Jamaica. Rishi Sunak dismissed a call for the government to apologise and pay reparations for the UK's historical role in slavery in 2023 after Bell Ribeiro-Addy asked if he would make a "full and meaningful apology" and "commit to reparatory justice".Sunak replied with a "no", and said: "Trying to unpick our history is not the right way forward."In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer ruled out compensation for the UK's historical role in the slave trade.At the time, he said he wanted to focus on the future of the Commonwealth. Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of people they had enslaved.The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

schema.headline: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but rules out reparations

title: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs
description: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and
body: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec townByJessica MurphyCanada digital editor and Nadine YousifSenior Canada reporterAs you cross the Ottawa river into Témiscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon.The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests  filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country.Most of the mill‘s 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief. For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life. She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year. "It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack". In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period". Property values in Témiscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town. There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out."If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers. "There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary."Image source, BBC/Jessica MurphyImage caption, The paper mill has served as the economic engine of Témiscaming for over a century.At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth.But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of  Témiscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive."If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,” says Stéphane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill. That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people.The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it.They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France. The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017. "We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall.But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support. Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge. In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers.Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Stéphane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in Témiscaming.Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada". He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free.And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken". "We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back." Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos.This month, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure. Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024. Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; £4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said.Sébastien Lemire, the elected MP for Témiscaming from the Bloc Québécois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly.A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas.It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets. On the Témiscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars."Image source, Supplied/Stéphane LefebvreImage caption, Témiscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry. In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes. Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs. The Témiscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US.Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in Témiscaming. Frank Dottori has been through all of this before. Now in his 80s and retired in Témiscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO.Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support. But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma.Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold."Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they organise themselves," he said. Image source, BBC/Nadine YousifImage caption, Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the Témiscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term.Many workers in Témiscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump — whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls — to ease some of his tariffs on Canada."We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too."There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at Témiscaming's mill, however.Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult.In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens."We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."

schema.headline: The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs

title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal."Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.Dressing like their stateSome candidates, like Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who represents Washington's 3rd Congressional District, are embracing a relaxed, outdoorsy image.The former car repair shop owner is up for re-election on a platform focused on support for small businesses and working families, after capturing a Republican-held seat in her state in 2022. She favours low fuss, low-key work jackets, flannel shirts, jeans and practical footwear.Robert Ordway, conservative public policy adviser and former owner of Capitol Hill Clothiers, says Gluesenkamp Perez is probably the most "spot-on" when it comes to "authenticity and where you come from"."Also it really vibes with the Pacific Northwest, which has trees and forests and a little bit more of an outdoor vibe," he says.Her style also "shepherds a message championing the working class", says Tashira Halyard, an attorney, content creator, and public policy expert based in Washington DC.Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Gluesenkamp Perez chooses a workwear-inspired wardrobeDemocratic lawmaker Mary Peltola, running for a Senate seat in the battleground state of Alaska, takes a similar approach.She made headlines for wearing traditional boots of the Yup'ik people while being sworn in as a congresswoman in 2022.During this election cycle, her rugged outdoor gear nods to her days working on a fishing boat on Alaska's Kuskokwim River and her "fish, family and freedom" campaign slogan.The flannels, puffer jackets and indigenous-inspired details seem designed to remind voters that Peltola is a native (and Native) Alaskan, says conservative author and journalist Bonnie Kristian.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Mary Peltola wore the traditional footwear of the Yup'ik people when she was sworn inPatriotism on their sleevesOther candidates, such as Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson of Iowa, have been opting for a bolder, patriotic image.While polished and conservative, her style of dress has included classic, arguably nostalgic touches, including denim and bandanas for more casual appearances.In a tight race against her Democratic opponent, Hinson has tried to separate herself from specific policy decisions made by the Trump administration but has still expressed loyalty to the president.She slipped into pumps with the American flag bedazzled across them at a primary election party in Iowa in June. The look, reminiscent of the style worn by Trump supporters at rallies, is quintessential American patriotism, according to Halyard."Ashley's American flag high heels, denim dress and bright red blouse worn with a bandana around her neck are classic Americana," she says."It's this idea that… I'm literally going to wear my patriotism on my sleeve."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Ashley Hinson's campaign style is inspired by the American flag Journalist Bonnie Kristian says there is "a strategic advantage" to Hinson's look, one in which she is "cultivating a visual identity that cannot possibly be misinterpreted" in an era where social media presence, if only for a split second, is crucial."Her denim dress, red bandana and sparkly American flag shoes all signal that she's a Republican wooing rural voters - and indeed she is."Tie off, cowboy boots onOnce a reliable Republican stronghold, Texas has become a battleground between top prosecutor Ken Paxton, 63, who was controversially endorsed by Trump over a longtime senator, and Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico, 37.On the campaign trail, both contenders have been making similar clothing choices, wearing relaxed blazers and cowboy boots.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite political differences, Talarico, left, and Paxton have similar wardrobes"The necktie is dead on the campaign trail in both parties," says Ordway."The younger man dresses up to look serious, and the older man dresses down to look like one of the guys."Fashion critic Friedman notes that Talarico's handcrafted Lucchese cowboy boots "are a very deliberate choice that allows him to speak to all different kinds of constituencies in Texas"."Those boots mean something that is very deeply rooted in Texas semiology," Friedman says, referring to the study of signs and their interpretations. "Former US President George W Bush wore Lucchese cowboy boots, so suddenly you're crossing all sorts of party lines and tapping into all sorts of different electoral groups with your shoes."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Former US president George W Bush was a fan of cowboy bootsMeanwhile, Paxton's style of dress has come under fire on more than one front. It has drawn the disapproval of Trump who has urged voters to focus on his record because it "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great".The Republican candidate has also been criticised by his opponent for wearing a pricey watch and polo shirt from the luxury hotel chain Four Seasons as a debate about the high cost of living dominates the midterms."The criticism around his apparent luxury watch and Four Seasons polo raises another style-branded question: casual clothes don't necessarily communicate an ordinary lifestyle," says Zee, a stylist and faculty associate at Arizona State University's Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising."A five-star resort-branded polo can carry luxury associations just as clearly as a suit. "The watch's identity and value were unconfirmed, but the perception illustrates how an accessory can complicate a candidate's message," he explains.Image source, Facebook/KenPaxtonTXImage caption, Paxton's watch and Four Seasons polo shirt drew criticismPersonal uniformsA uniform, if it reads naturally, is an incredibly effective tool, says Friedman, and a great way to be recognised across the country.It's an approach adopted by Republican Senator and former congresswoman for Tennessee's 7th congressional district, Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor of her state.Senator Blackburn is often seen in structured jackets and skirts, sometimes with patterns. Ordway remembers that Blackburn "was extremely polished" whenever he spotted her in Capitol Hill while working there as a legislative director for a former Indiana senator."I always saw pearls on her," he says. "Since she's a veteran politician I think how she dresses in relation to how voters see her was probably decided many, many years ago."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Marsha Blackburn has been wearing a consistent style for decades"Her looks tend to be fairly timeless - we could imagine GOP women wearing many of them any time in the last three decades," Kristian adds.Meanwhile, Michigan Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a highly competitive race against a Trump-backed former congressman, has adopted a consistent look of black V-neck T-shirt and blue jeans.The left-wing political outsider, whose campaign slogan is "money out of politics, money in your pocket", refers to his outfit choices as "minimal look, maximal politics". The effect, says Ordway, is reminiscent of a start-up entrepreneur, designed to appeal to an urban, working-class electorate.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdul El-Sayed calls his outfit "minimal look, maximal politics"It also removes much of the "ceremony of a political appearance", Zee says."The suggestion is that attention should go to what he is saying. But the plain T-shirt remains an image choice. Looking un-styled can still be a deliberate form of branding."Trump, master of the imageImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump's suit and red tie is instantly recognisableFriedman notes that the master of this look in the US at the moment is Trump. His instantly recognisable power suit and red tie, ever-present in film and reality TV, were cultivated even before he moved into the White House."[Trump] doesn't just have his own merch, but he's got his own outfit, and now he's got all his cabinet wearing the same outfit, and half the Senate is wearing his outfit, and it becomes like a Pavlovian signifier," Friedman says."If they're wearing a navy suit, red tie, and white shirt, you're like, 'oh, that's a Trump person,'" she says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wear similar looksWhatever the outcome of the elections for Trump and his party, Friedman expects to see more politicians effectively branding themselves with their clothing when the 2028 general election rolls in."What we see is that so much of politics now is fought over social media and over TV, and that places a premium on visual messaging that is only going to become more important."

schema.headline: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes

title: How to prepare for an emergency: What households in different countries stock up on
description: Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on
body: Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement."It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".Ayumi T, who lives in Tokyo, has kept an emergency bag for years in case of events like earthquakes, typhoons and extreme heat. But after an earthquake in 2024 killed hundreds of people and caused widespread damage to Japan's Noto Peninsula, Ayumi stocked up even more.Tokyo's government has a 68-page disaster prevention guide, external, which details what to keep in an emergency kit and what to do in certain emergency situations.In her emergency rucksack - kept in her wardrobe - Ayumi keeps clothes, towels, menstrual products, disposable chopsticks, sticky notes, disposable masks and a disposable toilet, like those used by hikers and campers."A lot of it is old stuff I don't use anymore," Ayumi, 27, who works at a university, says.Every new year, her family check their kits and update them if necessary, replacing out-of-date food, for example.Over the past five years, "it's been on my mind, 'what happens in case of emergency?'", Nicole Bonds says.The leadership coach in Atlanta, puts this down to noticing "significantly more and more" severe weather patterns and storms around the world and a lack of preparedness.Her motto is "don't panic, be prepared", she says.As well as a large selection of cleaning and hygiene products, Nicole, 48, has bought batteries, a power bank, first-aid supplies, rechargeable fans, blankets and sleeping bags.To keep it affordable she picks up a small amount of supplies "here and there" to gradually build up her stock. She keeps some of the items under her bed, in packing bags and in her kitchen cabinets.Where Michael Stuut lives in the Netherlands is below sea level. He says he worries about extreme weather but also possible war.The 39-year-old, who lives in Hoorn with his wife and five-year-old son, started preparing his kit a few years ago.Michael keeps a healthy stash of power equipment as well as food - including a Starlink Mini, a small and lightweight satellite device for internet access.He keeps supplies in his attic and a crawl space under the house - here lies about 120 litres of water, cash, a first-aid kit and a generator.Earlier this year, Michael created an app to log his food supplies and when they might expire."Being prepared isn't about panic," he says. "It's about being the calm one when the lights go out."In late 2025, Dutch authorities launched a campaign that instructed households to have 72 hours' worth of supplies, much like UK authorities have just done.At the beginning of his prepping journey, Michael's wife didn't see the need, but he says she now understands the importance. They've told their five-year-old the supplies are simply for when they don't want to go to the shop, adding they "don't want to burden him".Michael is sceptical of the three-day advice - also recommended by the UK - but says: "Every household that has a few basic things at home makes it easier for the emergency services to help the people who need it most."Additional reporting by Hanae Takahashi and Richard Frost

schema.headline: How to prepare for an emergency: What households in different countries stock up on

title: Spain train disaster clouds Pedro Sánchez chances of re-election
description: The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative
body: The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid."They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop."I'm no judge... But these are the facts."So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister."I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading."This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails -  very different to the latest collision.But there is a similar impact."It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.That's when Sánchez called an early election.His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox."They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.Suddenly, the tone has changed."They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."There is also anger.There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.Here in Toledo, the mood is nervous."We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government."This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too."This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

schema.headline: Spain train disaster clouds Pedro Sánchez chances of re-election

title: Everton striker Thierno Barry's relief family not home during burglary
description: Everton striker Thierno Barry has said he was relieved that his family were not at home when it was burgled while he played in a cup match. His home i
body: Everton striker Thierno Barry has said he was relieved that his family were not at home when it was burgled while he played in a cup match. His home in Greater Manchester was targeted while he was playing for Everton against Newcastle United in a Carabao Cup tie at the Hill Dickinson stadium on Thursday. The Frenchman, 24, posted on Instagram "things could have been much worse" had his partner and toddler not been in the stands.A spokesman for Greater Manchester Police said an investigation was ongoing. Barry posted that he would not put his family "at risk" in the future by posting about his life on social media.He said: "Maybe I've been too open about my family's life and mine, potentially putting them at risk, all just to show my lifestyle and inspire others through my journey and success, hoping to motivate them to do the same."My childhood was never easy, but I've always believed that when you give yourself the best possible chances, there is always hope."Unfortunately, in life, there are people and things beyond our control."

schema.headline: Everton striker Thierno Barry's relief family not home during burglary
